claims.text: A two-step thermomechanical route combining severe plastic deformation with a short recovery anneal can produce a tailored bimodal grain structure in high-entropy alloys.
A tailored bimodal grain structure will improve the combination of strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance relative to homogeneous processing.
Cast or homogenized high-entropy alloys typically have relatively uniform grain-size distributions.
Sufficient severe plastic deformation refines part of the alloy microstructure.
A short controlled recovery anneal can coarsen grains selectively while retaining fine grains elsewhere.
Solid-solution strengthening and sluggish diffusion make some high-entropy alloys suitable for processing-induced microstructural tailoring.
Excessive annealing can cause full grain growth and eliminate the desired grain-size heterogeneity.
Insufficient deformation will fail to generate the microstructural heterogeneity required by the hypothesis.
Ultrafine grains hinder dislocation motion and thereby increase yield strength.
Ultrafine grains increase stiffness or Young's modulus.
Coarser grains accommodate strain and thereby improve ductility.
Coarser grains promote crack deflection and crack blunting, thereby improving fracture resistance or toughness.
Spatial grain-size heterogeneity permits strengthening and strain-accommodation mechanisms to operate simultaneously.
Conventionally processed high-entropy alloys with uniform grain structures exhibit a strength-ductility trade-off.
The proposed processing route could improve yield strength by approximately 10–20% relative to the state of the art.
The proposed processing route could improve fracture resistance by approximately 10–20% relative to the state of the art.
The proposed processing route is expected to enhance ductility without a significant loss of stiffness.
Differences in alloy diffusion, phase stability, secondary phases, or segregation can prevent or alter the predicted response.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome quantifies an approximately 10–20% improvement only for yield strength and fracture resistance, while the falsification rule additionally requires at least approximately 10% improvement in ductility. Thus, the falsification criterion imposes a quantitative ductility prediction that is not stated in the predicted outcome.
